chapter_theme: Padumai, revived, looks at her healer and falls at once into love's sickness; the palace honours Civakan with bath, meal and betel, the king tests and praises his learning, and the chapter closes on the two lovers' separate sleepless laments on the same night.

cast.role: the hero, who cured Padumai of the snakebite
the king's daughter, bitten by a snake in the garden and revived by Civakan
the king, Padumai's father (named in the verses only as மன்னன்)
the palace serving women who attend Civakan at the king's order
the onlookers who watch Civakan revive Padumai

1291.reading: The narrator tells that Padumai, once she had looked at Civakan, at once lost her restraint, her modesty, her dark glow and her beauty, let her bangles slip, was covered over in a gold-coloured pallor, and made herself a quiver for Kama's arrows, she whose eyes were like the twin spears of Murugan raised in battle.
1291.event: Padumai, revived from the snakebite, looks at Civakan and is at once overcome by love.
1291.nuance: The first thing the cured girl does is look, and the look undoes in one line the whole list the akam books treat as a woman's defences (நிறை, நாண்) together with the signs the Kural gives to separation (slipping bangles, பசலை); here they come at the first sight, not after parting.

1292.reading: The narrator says she was seized again by the snake of desire, whose fangs are the look of sword-like eyes and whose venom is a fierce fire, the snake that dwells within the anthill called the body, ruled by the master of the five senses.
1292.event: Padumai, just freed of the snake's poison, is struck anew by desire.
1292.nuance: மீட்டும் ('again') ties the figure to the plot: the girl has just been cured of a real snakebite, and the poet makes her love a second bite. The anthill of the body and the five senses (ஐம்பொறி) are the yogic and ascetic image of the body; whose eyes give the bite is not said, and வாட்கண் is usually a woman's epithet.

1293.reading: As she swooned and sighed hotly, her companions and mothers, women with fragrant garlands, gathered round and told Civakan, whom they liken to an adorned elephant, that if he touched her the poison would go, and blessed him.
1293.event: Padumai faints again, and her companions and mothers beg Civakan to touch her and drive out the poison.
1293.nuance: The women read the swoon of love as a return of the venom; the reader, told in 1292 that the second snake is desire, sees that their remedy (his touch) is the right one for the wrong reason.

1294.reading: Thinking that if she saw him, heard his firm words or felt his touch her life would hold, Civakan stroked the jewelled girl all over her body, as if spreading cool sandal paste on her.
1294.event: Civakan strokes Padumai's whole body to keep her alive.
1294.nuance: The three channels he counts on (sight, speech, touch) are the senses through which love entered in 1291 and 1292; the cure goes in by the same doors as the sickness.

1295.reading: Then the girl of flawless, nectar-sweet speech, with a look of her wide sword-like eyes that looked as though it did not look, wound round the generous man and bound him fast.
1295.event: Padumai binds Civakan with a covert glance.
1295.nuance: உற்ற நோக்கம் உறாததொர் நோக்கு, a look that touches and seems not to, is the akam convention of the averted glance; here it is not a sign to be read but the cord that ties him.

1296.reading: Some said he was a Vidyadhara hero, some that he was a prince of the gods, some that no one but he could have brought back a life that was ebbing away, and some that the great-crowned king of the old walled city would give the maiden this very day to the man with the deadly spear.
1296.event: Onlookers debate who Civakan is and foretell that the king will give him his daughter.
1296.nuance: Each guess is introduced by என்பார், 'some say'; the crowd does not know who he is, and the hero keeps his identity hidden in this ilampakam.

1297.reading: Other women stood saying to a friend that if one could lie with this man, having painted his chest with one's breasts, as lightning plays round the young white crescent in a bright sky and as gold chains play over a rich necklace, then even a woman's wavering birth would be sweet.

claims.claim: a woman's birth is a wavering, unsettled lot, made sweet only by union with such a man

1297.nuance: துளங்கு பெண் பிறப்பு, 'the trembling birth of a woman', is said in passing as common knowledge; the women do not argue it, they only name the one thing that would redeem it.

1298.reading: Women of sweet speech and bright smiles were bewildered, asking who the jewelled women might be who, having done rare penance, would be born to sleep on this noble man's chest and bind him with their womanhood, and saying that with their own dark eyes they too had now seen Kama.

claims.claim: union with a worthy husband is the fruit of rare penance done in a former life

1298.nuance: அருந்தவஞ் செய்து வந்த, 'who came having done rare penance', puts the marriage the story will bring under the law of merit from a past life; the speakers are bewildered onlookers, and the verse does not mark the claim as the poet's.

1299.reading: At the king's command the fair women praised the youth with his garland of many flowers, rubbed him with scented oil, bathed him in clear water, and brought in red-gold caskets clothes, sandal paste, sweet incense and flowers with their vessels.
1299.event: By the king's order the palace women bathe and anoint Civakan and bring him clothes and perfumes.

1300.reading: Wearing wooden sandals inlaid with gold and with a gleaming gem knob at the front, he went and reached the rare hall decked with chosen garlands, where the women with flowered bangles honoured him and set out golden vessels.
1300.event: Civakan goes in jewelled sandals to the garlanded hall, where the women lay out golden dishes.
1300.nuance: Line 1 (ஏந்திய வேற்பத் தாங்கி) does not divide clearly; the reading of the opening phrase is a guess, and the sandals and the hall are the verse's sure content.

1301.reading: After maidens had washed his golden feet with water from pitchers, as one washes lotuses, he rinsed his mouth well, sat high on a seat of sweet flowers and ate the nectar-like food with pleasure, he who was the god of spring to spear-eyed women in bright jewels.
1301.event: Civakan's feet are washed and he sits on a flower seat and eats.

1302.reading: When fragrant powder and water were brought, he took them, washed off, sipped water from his palm three times, wiped his mouth three times so no stain was left, touched the parts of his face with his fingers, smoothed his palm with a cloth, and sat, splendid to see.
1302.event: After the meal Civakan performs the mouth-rinsing in full.
1302.nuance: The poet slows the story for the full after-meal rite, three sips, three wipings and the fingers to the face, the very sequence a rule book of conduct sets out; the hero's correctness at table is part of what the king is watching before he tests his learning in 1303.

1303.reading: When the hero with warrior's anklets had taken betel and areca from a well-made red-gold pouch and held it in his cheek, the king of the warring spear asked him about all the arts, heard his answers, and said that on earth there was no equal to this man who was like the great sea.
1303.event: The king questions Civakan on every art and declares him peerless on earth.
1303.nuance: The king tests the stranger's learning only after he has been bathed, fed and given betel; the honour comes before the examination, and the verdict is spoken by the father whose daughter's hand is at stake.

1304.reading: The sun set, the long many-jewelled lamps were lit, instruments sounded, the prince climbed onto the soft couch heaped with cushions, and his thoughts grew intent.
1304.event: At nightfall Civakan goes to his couch, his mind turning on Padumai.
1304.nuance: கூர்ந்தது சிந்தையே closes the public day and opens the private night; what his thought turns to is left for the next verses to say.

1305.reading: Her breasts, as if unable to bear his gaze there, swelled hot and rose, her waist gave way and wilted as if asking what this was, and her hips spread wider than men who keep no measure.
1305.nuance: The verse has no first-person mark; it is read as the start of Civakan's night thoughts because 1306 and 1307 speak as 'I', but it may be the narrator's. The simile of line 4 (பாங்கிலாரின்) is a reading of a compressed phrase.

1306.reading: Civakan says that the tender budding breasts of the girl with fragrant long hair, swelling in their nature, stand there to distress, her slender waist melts, and the side-glance of that painted doll torments his life.

1307.reading: Civakan says that the smoke-perfumed flower-cloth on her raised hips, the jewelled girdle and her thick hair where honeyed buds open have all turned enemy to wretched him and breed a spreading sickness.

1308.reading: Civakan asks whether it is her flower bow, her fighting spear-like eyes, her speech full of sweetness or her innocent look, says he cannot tell which, and concludes that it is desire itself that churns him through love for her who is like a goddess who afflicts.
1308.nuance: After the list of 'or's he moves the cause from her to himself: the subject of கடைகின்றது is காமம், not any feature of hers.

1309.reading: While the prince there suffered a sinking grief, the girl with the garland of bright flowers, there too, melted like butter set above hot embers and was barely alive.
1309.event: Civakan and Padumai, in separate rooms, both waste with longing.
1309.nuance: The repeated அவ்வழி ('there', 'there too') sets the two nights side by side; the poet now turns from his lament to hers.

1310.reading: The girl with a waist like lightning flickering in rain and eyes like gleaming fish lay, while good women saluted her, in the soft bed made for her pleasure, like a doll fashioned by Maya.
1310.event: Padumai lies motionless in her bed.
1310.nuance: மயன் இழைத்த பாவை, a doll made by the divine craftsman, gives her beauty and her stillness at once: she lies as lifeless as a figure.

1311.reading: Padumai asks her maidens whether the thief who clung to her heart and took her restraint is Kama with his bending bow and long arrows, or the young god of the dark hill on the fragrant flower, saying she does not know, and begs them to tell her.
1311.nuance: நிறைகொண்ட கள்வன், 'the thief who took my restraint', names the loss of 1291 from inside. Which god மைவரை மைந்தன் means (perhaps Murugan) the verse does not settle.

1312.reading: Padumai seems to say that her life, which has no one else, now lies with him who, as if he had embraced her fully with his lovely swelling shoulders like gate-posts, drew out the pain lodged in her breast.
1312.nuance: Line 3 ends மீட்டவள் (feminine), where the sense seems to want the man who saved her; the verse may instead mean 'my life is in the waist of her who was saved', so the reading is tentative.

1313.reading: Padumai says her heart is like the great sea whose water was churned and tossed when those seeking undying nectar gathered and, with knowledge, used the mountain as a churning stick.
1313.nuance: The churning of the ocean for nectar is a Puranic story the Jain poet uses as plain ornament; the nectar sought points back to the life she has been given and the man who gave it.

1314.reading: The laughing white moon, the anril in the palmyra frond, the low bell of the fine white bull, the hostile evening and the water-lily that brings grief all burn like a smokeless blazing fire.
1314.nuance: The list is the akam evening of separation (the anril, the herd's bell, the moon); no first person marks the speaker, and it is read as Padumai's lament continuing from 1311 to 1313.

1315.reading: The narrator says her sighs withered the round flower garlands strewn on her soft bed, and for the lovely girl, sick with the love her own eyes had given her, the length of the night passed like a year.
1315.event: Padumai spends a sleepless night of longing that seems a year long.
1315.nuance: தன் கண் தரு காமநோய், 'the love-sickness her eyes gave', brings the chapter back to 1291, where the trouble began with her look.

links.note: In 1290 the poison leaves Padumai's body as darkness breaks before the sun; two verses later she is bitten again by the snake of desire.
links.teaches: The poet makes the cure the cause of a new sickness: the instant the real venom is drawn out, the girl's first look at her healer lets in a second venom, so the rescue and the love are one event told twice.

links.note: The god foretold that the king who guards the earth would give Civakan his flawless daughter; the onlookers now say the king will give him the maiden today.
links.teaches: The prophecy reaches the crowd as gossip: what the god told Civakan privately is now guessed aloud by strangers who do not even know who he is, so the story's foreknowledge passes from the divine to the public before the king has spoken.

links.note: The onlookers guess whether he is a Vidyadhara hero or a prince of the gods; Padumai asks her maidens whether he is Kama or a young god, and says she does not know.
links.teaches: The question of the stranger's identity, a public puzzle in 1296, becomes in the girl's mouth a symptom of love: her not knowing who he is is now part of her sickness, since she cannot even name the thief.

links.note: Civakan says desire churns him (கடைகின்றது காமமே); Padumai says her heart is the ocean churned for nectar.
links.teaches: The poet gives the two lovers, lying apart on the same night, one verb: he says it plainly of himself, and she expands it into the whole churning of the ocean, so the image binds their separate laments into a matched pair.

links.note: Tirumular's single five-hooded serpent lives in the anthill of enjoyment and, its hoods drawn into one, makes the body its fit home; the epic's snake of desire lives in the anthill of the body ruled by the five senses and bites again.
links.teaches: Both poets house a serpent of the five senses in the body's anthill, but Tirumular's can be stilled by discipline into one hood while the epic's strikes the moment a spell has cured the real snake, showing that a remedy for poison is no remedy for the senses.

gains.a: a yogic reading of its anthill and five senses, which makes the love-bite a statement about the body and not only an ornament
gains.b: a narrative case where the serpent of the senses is shown striking in a living person, against which its taming is measured

links.note: The Kural's man says she will not look at him directly but smiles as if narrowing one eye; the epic says Padumai bound Civakan with a look that looked as if it did not look.
links.teaches: The averted look that the Kural treats as a sign the man must decode becomes in the epic an act with an effect: the same not-quite-glance does not hint at love, it ties the hero fast, so the convention moves from evidence to force.

gains.a: the convention behind its paradoxical look, which shows the line is a known sign and not a fresh conceit
gains.b: a scene in which the half-look is followed by its consequence, the man bound, which the couplet leaves unstated

links.note: The Kural says penance is striven for here because what is desired is obtained as desired; the onlookers say only women who did rare penance before could be born to sleep on Civakan's chest.
links.teaches: The onlookers take the couplet's promise at its word and fill 'whatever is desired' with a husband's embrace, showing how the motive the Kural offers for penance could be heard as making penance the price of pleasure in the next birth.

gains.a: a doctrinal rule behind its onlookers' wonder, that what is gained now is the fruit of penance done before
gains.b: a concrete example of what ordinary people wanted penance to bring, which tests how wide the couplet's 'whatever is desired' is meant to be

links.note: The Acharakkovai sets out the mouth-rinsing the great have seen as the way: three sips, wiping, and touching the face's parts with the fingers; Civakan sips three times, wipes three times and touches his face with his fingers.
links.teaches: The rule book's after-meal rinse appears in the epic, step for step, as a mark of the hero's breeding, performed under the eyes of a king who will next examine him, so the code of conduct works in the story as a credential.

gains.a: the source of its unusually exact sequence, which shows the poet is narrating a known rite and not inventing detail
gains.b: a scene showing the rite performed by a prince as a sign of refinement, beyond the bare prescription

links.note: The Acharakkovai lists what one does not do in a great man's house: spit, climb a high seat, chew areca, speak out of turn, lie down; in the king's house Civakan sits on a high flower seat, chews areca and lies on a couch.
links.teaches: Civakan does three of the five things forbidden in a great man's house, and does them at the king's command, so the pair shows that the rule binds the dependent and the visitor and is suspended for an honoured guest whom the host himself seats, serves and beds.

gains.a: the rule against which its hospitality reads as a deliberate honour and not a mere list of comforts
gains.b: a limit to the rule: the prohibitions assume a lower visitor, and the host's own gift lifts them

links.note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe and answers that it has all three; Civakan asks whether it is her bow, her eyes, her speech or her look and says he cannot tell.
links.teaches: Both men ask the same 'is it this or that' of a woman who wounds them, but the Kural settles the question in her look, while Civakan gives it up and lays the cause on his own desire, so the epic turns the couplet's question about her into an admission about himself.

gains.a: the convention of the bewildered list of alternatives, which shows the force of its refusal to answer
gains.b: an alternative ending to the convention, in which the cause moves from the woman's look to the man's longing

links.note: The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; Padumai finds the bull's bell, the moon, the anril and the evening burning like smokeless fire.
links.teaches: The evening's pastoral sounds that burn the parted wife of the Kural are given to a girl who has not yet been joined or parted, showing that the epic transfers the whole thurai of evening grief to the first night after first sight.

gains.a: the source convention of its list, which shows the bull's bell and the evening as the settled tokens of separation
gains.b: a case where the separation grief is felt before any union, widening the occasion the couplet presupposes

links.note: The Kural's woman asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave the unending sickness; the epic says Padumai lay sick with the love her own eyes had given her.
links.teaches: The couplet's blame of the eyes is spoken long after, by a woman left alone; the epic places the same diagnosis on the very first night, so the eyes are blamed before the love has any history.

gains.a: the convention that the eyes are the cause and so the culprit, which gives தன் கண் தரு its edge
gains.b: an instance of the eyes' guilt at the start of love, where the couplet knows it only in separation

source_issues: Verses 1291, 1296, 1297, 1298, 1299 and 1303 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 1300 line 1 (ஏந்திய வேற்பத் தாங்கி) does not divide into clear words, and line 3 begins யாயந்தநன், probably for ஆய்ந்த நன்.
Verse 1303 line 1 reads செம்பெர் னடைப்பை, apparently a misprint for செம்பொன் அடைப்பை.
Verse 1312 line 3 ends மீட்டவ/ளிடைய (மீட்டவள்), feminine, where the sense seems to want the masculine; the line may be corrupt.
